qs.q: What is a process?

c.x: A program stored on disk that has not been loaded yet
A program in execution, historically also known as a job
A data structure that stores information about a program
A system program that is associated with the operating system

qs.e: A process is a program in execution (historically called a job). The OS keeps the information about each process in a data structure called the PCB. Process = program in execution

qs.q: Which pair of items represents the current status of a process?

c.x: The value of the program counter and the contents of the processor's registers
The contents of the text section and the contents of the heap section
The contents of the ready queue and the contents of the wait queue
The value of the process number and the list of open files

qs.e: The current status of a process is represented by the value of the program counter (PC) and the contents of the processor's registers. PC + registers

qs.q: Which option correctly matches each section of a process with what it stores?

c.x: Text: global variables; data: executable code; heap: dynamically allocated variables; stack: local variables
Text: executable code; data: dynamically allocated variables; heap: global variables; stack: local variables
Text: executable code; data: global variables; heap: dynamically allocated variables; stack: local variables
Text: executable code; data: global variables; heap: local variables; stack: dynamically allocated variables

qs.e: The text section holds the executable code, the data section holds global variables, the heap holds dynamically allocated variables, and the stack holds temporary (local) variables. Text = code, data = globals, heap = dynamic, stack = locals

qs.q: A variable is allocated dynamically while the program is running. Which section of the process holds it?

c.x: Text section
Data section
Stack section
Heap section

qs.e: Dynamically allocated variables live in the heap section. Global variables are in the data section, and local (temporary) variables are in the stack section. Heap section

qs.q: In the process memory layout, which sections are placed at the highest address and at the lowest address?

c.x: Text at the highest address; stack at the lowest address
Stack at the highest address; text at the lowest address
Heap at the highest address; data at the lowest address
Data at the highest address; heap at the lowest address

qs.e: In the layout diagram the stack is at the top (max) and the text section is at the bottom (0), with the data and heap sections above the text. The stack and the heap grow toward each other. Stack at the top, text at the bottom

qs.q: In which state is a process that is waiting to be assigned to a processor?

c.x: New
Waiting
Ready
Terminated

qs.e: A ready process is waiting to be assigned to a processor. A waiting process is waiting for some event to occur. Ready

qs.q: A process has requested data from the disk and cannot continue until the transfer completes. In which state is it?

c.x: Waiting
Ready
Running
Terminated

qs.e: The process is waiting for an I/O event to occur, so it is in the waiting state. It is not ready, because even with a free CPU it could not make progress. Waiting

qs.q: Which event moves a process from the running state to the ready state?

c.x: Scheduler dispatch
I/O or event wait
Admitted
Interrupt

qs.e: In the state diagram, an interrupt moves a process from running to ready. Scheduler dispatch moves it from ready to running, and I/O or event wait moves it from running to waiting. Interrupt: running → ready

qs.q: A process in the waiting state receives the I/O or event it was waiting for. What happens next?

c.x: It moves directly to the running state
It moves to the ready state
It moves to the terminated state
It returns to the new state

qs.e: On I/O or event completion the process goes from waiting to ready. It must then wait for the scheduler to dispatch it before it runs again. Waiting → ready

qs.q: A process is admitted, gets the CPU, requests I/O, completes the I/O, gets the CPU again, and then finishes. Which sequence of states is correct?

c.x: new → running → waiting → ready → running → terminated
new → ready → waiting → running → ready → terminated
new → ready → running → waiting → ready → running → terminated
new → ready → running → waiting → running → terminated

e: Admitted: new → ready.
Scheduler dispatch: ready → running.
I/O or event wait: running → waiting.
I/O or event completion: waiting → ready (never directly to running).
Scheduler dispatch again: ready → running.
Exit: running → terminated.
<mark>new → ready → running → waiting → ready → running → terminated</mark>

qs.q: Which of the following transitions is <u>not</u> shown in the process state diagram?

c.x: New to ready (admitted)
Running to waiting (I/O or event wait)
Ready to running (scheduler dispatch)
Waiting to running (scheduler dispatch)

qs.e: A waiting process must first return to the ready state; there is no direct arrow from waiting to running. <mark>Waiting → running does not exist</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes a PCB?

c.x: A data structure that stores information about one process and is kept by the OS
A region in the process address space that stores its local variables
A queue that holds all processes waiting to execute on a CPU
A system call that a parent process uses to create a child process

qs.e: Each process is represented in the OS by a process control block (PCB), also known as a task control block: a data structure that stores information about that process. PCB = per-process information record

qs.q: A running process is stopped by the OS and must later continue exactly where it left off. Where does the OS find the data needed to restart it?

c.x: In the text section of the process
In the PCB of the process
In the header of the ready queue
In the mailbox of the process

qs.e: The OS uses the process's PCB to store all the data needed to start (or restart) the process, along with accounting data. PCB

qs.q: Which option correctly matches PCB fields with their contents?

c.x: Program counter: state saved when an interrupt occurs; CPU registers: address of the next instruction; memory-management information: process location in memory
Program counter: address of the next instruction; CPU registers: process location in memory; memory-management information: state saved when an interrupt occurs
Program counter: address of the next instruction; CPU registers: state saved when an interrupt occurs; memory-management information: process location in memory
Program counter: process location in memory; CPU registers: address of the next instruction; memory-management information: state saved when an interrupt occurs

qs.e: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, the CPU registers store state information when an interrupt occurs, and the memory-management information gives the process location in memory. PC = next instruction, registers = saved state, memory info = location

qs.q: The OS needs to know which I/O devices are allocated to a process and which files it has open. Which PCB field provides this?

c.x: Accounting information
CPU-scheduling information
Process state
I/O status information

qs.e: I/O status information contains the allocated I/O devices, open files, and so on. I/O status information

qs.q: Which of the following is <u>not</u> stored in a PCB?

c.x: The executable code of the process
Scheduling parameters such as priority
Accounting information such as time limits
The process state such as new or ready

qs.e: A PCB stores the process state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling, memory-management, accounting and I/O status information. The executable code belongs to the text section of the process. Executable code is not in the PCB

qs.q: What does the degree of multiprogramming mean?

c.x: The number of cores available in the system
The number of processes waiting for I/O to complete
The number of processes in memory
The number of processes that terminate each second

qs.e: The degree of multiprogramming is the number of processes in memory. <mark>Number of processes in memory</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes?

c.x: An I/O-bound process spends more time computing; a CPU-bound process spends more time doing I/O
An I/O-bound process spends more time doing I/O; a CPU-bound process spends more time computing
Both spend most of their time doing I/O, but a CPU-bound process uses more cores
Both spend most of their time computing, but an I/O-bound process has a larger PCB

qs.e: An I/O-bound process spends more of its time doing I/O, while a CPU-bound process uses more of its time doing computations. I/O-bound = mostly I/O; CPU-bound = mostly computation

qs.q: A system has 4 cores and 9 ready processes. What happens to the 5 excess processes?

c.x: They are terminated by the CPU scheduler to save memory
They are moved to an I/O wait queue until devices are free
They run in parallel by sharing the registers of the 4 cores
They wait in the ready queue until a core is free

qs.e: If there are more ready processes than cores, the excess processes have to wait (in the ready queue) until a core is free and they can be rescheduled. <mark>Excess processes wait until a core is free</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares the ready queue and the wait queue?

c.x: Ready queue: processes waiting to execute on a CPU; wait queue: processes waiting for an event to occur
Ready queue: processes waiting for an event to occur; wait queue: processes waiting to execute on a CPU
Ready queue: processes that have finished execution; wait queue: processes that are still being created
Ready queue: only the process that is now running; wait queue: all other processes in memory

qs.e: The ready queue contains processes waiting to execute on a CPU, and the wait queue contains processes waiting for a certain event to occur. Ready queue = waiting for CPU; wait queue = waiting for an event

qs.q: According to the queuing diagram, where does a running process go after it issues an I/O request?

c.x: The ready queue
The I/O wait queue
The child termination wait queue
The interrupt wait queue

qs.e: After an I/O request the process is placed in the I/O wait queue. When the I/O completes, it returns to the ready queue. I/O request → I/O wait queue

qs.q: In the queuing diagram, a running process creates a child process. Where does it wait until the child terminates?

c.x: The I/O wait queue
The interrupt wait queue
The child termination wait queue
The ready queue

qs.e: After creating a child, the process waits in the child termination wait queue; when the child terminates it goes back to the ready queue. Create child → child termination wait queue

qs.q: In the queuing diagram, the time slice of a running process expires. Where does the process go?

c.x: The I/O wait queue
The interrupt wait queue
The child termination wait queue
The ready queue

qs.e: When the time slice expires, the process is not waiting for any event, so it goes straight back to the ready queue. Time slice expired → ready queue

qs.q: In the lecture's context-switch example, process $P_0$ is executing when an interrupt or system call occurs, and the CPU then switches to process $P_1$. What does the OS do in between?

c.x: It saves the state of $P_0$ into $PCB_0$, then reloads the state from $PCB_1$
It saves the state of $P_0$ into $PCB_1$, then reloads the state from $PCB_0$
It reloads the state from $PCB_1$, then saves the state of $P_0$ into $PCB_0$
It saves the state of $P_1$ into $PCB_0$, then reloads the state from $PCB_1$

e: An interrupt or system call occurs while $P_0$ is executing, and the OS takes control.
The OS saves the current state of $P_0$ into its own PCB, $PCB_0$.
The OS reloads the saved state of $P_1$ from $PCB_1$.
$P_1$ executes, and later the same steps run in the opposite direction ($PCB_1$ saved, $PCB_0$ reloaded).
<mark>Save into PCB<sub>0</sub>, then reload from PCB<sub>1</sub></mark>

qs.q: Why is context-switch time considered pure overhead?

c.x: Because each switch terminates the running process and creates a new PCB
Because the CPU registers are cleared during the switch and never restored
Because the system does no useful work for any process while it switches
Because the switch can happen only after the running process has finished

qs.e: During a context switch the OS only saves one context and loads another, so no useful work is done for any process. <mark>No useful work while switching</mark>

qs.q: In the process tree shown on the slide, which process is a <u>direct child</u> of `logind` (pid 8415)?

c.x: `bash` (pid 8416)
`python` (pid 2808)
`tcsh` (pid 4005)

qs.e: In the tree, `logind` created `bash`, and `bash` created `ps` and `vim` (so `ps` is a grandchild). `python` is another child of `systemd`, and `tcsh` is in the `sshd` branch. <mark>bash is the direct child of logind</mark>

qs.q: A process creates several new processes. What are the creating process and the new processes called?

c.x: The creating process is the child; the new processes are its parents
The creating process is the owner; the new processes are its users
The creating process is the client; the new processes are its servers
The creating process is the parent; the new processes are its children

qs.e: The creating process is the parent, and the new processes are its children. Each child may in turn create other processes, which forms a tree. Parent creates children

qs.q: In terms of address space, which two possibilities exist for a newly created child process?

c.x: Either the child is a duplicate of the parent, or a new program is loaded into the child
Either the child shares the address space of the parent, or the parent is loaded into the child
Either the parent waits until its children terminate, or it executes concurrently with them
Either the parent and child share no resources, or they share all of the resources

qs.e: For the address space, the child is either a duplicate of the parent or has a new program loaded into it. The other options describe the execution possibilities and the resource-sharing possibilities. Duplicate of the parent, or a new program

qs.q: A parent process creates a child and then blocks until the child terminates. Which execution possibility is this?

c.x: The parent continues to execute concurrently with its children
The child process is a duplicate of the parent process
The parent waits until some or all of its children have terminated
The children share a subset of the parent's resources

qs.e: In terms of execution, the parent either runs concurrently with its children or waits until some or all of its children have terminated. Blocking until the child ends is the second case. Parent waits for its children

qs.q: A process finishes executing and asks the OS to delete it. Which system call does it use, and what does the OS do afterwards?

c.x: It uses abort, and the OS deallocates all of its resources
It uses exit, and the OS deallocates all of its resources
It uses exit, and the OS leaves its resources allocated until its parent terminates
It uses abort, and the OS leaves its resources allocated until its parent terminates

qs.e: A process that finishes execution asks the OS to delete it with the exit system call, and the OS then deallocates all of its resources. The abort call is used by a parent to terminate its child. exit, then resources deallocated

qs.q: Which of the following is <u>not</u> a case in which a parent may terminate its child using the abort system call?

c.x: The task assigned to the child is no longer required
The child has exceeded the usage of the resources allocated to it
The parent is exiting in a cascading termination system
The child has finished its task and has called exit

qs.e: A parent may abort a child when its task is no longer required, when it exceeds its allocated resources, or when the parent is exiting in a cascading termination system. A child that finishes and calls exit terminates normally. <mark>Normal exit is not an abort case</mark>

qs.q: In a system that uses cascading termination, a process $A$ terminates. $A$ has a child $B$, and $B$ has its own child $C$. What happens?

c.x: Both $B$ and $C$ are terminated as well
Only $B$ is terminated, and $C$ continues to run
Neither is terminated, and both become independent
Only $C$ is terminated, and $B$ continues to run

e: In cascading termination, if a process terminates, all of its children must be terminated as well.
When $A$ terminates, its child $B$ must be terminated.
Since $B$ terminates, its own child $C$ must also be terminated.
<mark>Both B and C are terminated</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares independent and cooperating processes?

c.x: An independent process shares data with other processes; a cooperating one shares no data with them
Both share data with other processes, but only a cooperating one needs an IPC mechanism
An independent process shares no data with other processes; a cooperating one shares data with them
Neither shares data, but a cooperating process can create children while an independent one cannot

qs.e: An independent process does not share data with other processes, whereas a cooperating process shares data with other executing processes and therefore needs an IPC mechanism. Cooperating processes share data

qs.q: A large task is broken into sub-tasks that run in parallel as separate cooperating processes. Which reason for process cooperation does this illustrate?

c.x: Information sharing
Computation speedup
Modularity
Resource allocation

qs.e: Breaking a task into sub-tasks that run in parallel is computation speedup. Information sharing is, for example, copying and pasting, and modularity means dividing the functions of a system into separate processes. Computation speedup

qs.q: Which statement about shared-memory communication is correct?

c.x: A process creates a shared-memory region in its address space, and other processes attach it to theirs
The OS creates the region and copies each message between the communicating processes
Processes exchange data only through send and receive operations managed by the OS
Each process stays restricted to its own memory and copies data through the kernel

qs.e: Normally the OS restricts a process to its own memory, but communicating processes agree to remove this restriction: one creates a shared region in its address space, others attach it, and they read and write data in it. <mark>Create a region, attach it, read and write</mark>

qs.q: In shared-memory communication, which task is the responsibility of the communicating processes themselves?

c.x: Creating the message queue that holds the data in the kernel
Blocking the sender until the message is received
Choosing which process the CPU executes next
Ensuring that they do not write to the same location simultaneously

qs.e: With shared memory the processes are responsible for determining the form of the data and its location, and for making sure they are <u>not</u> writing to the same location simultaneously. <mark>The processes must avoid simultaneous writes</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares shared memory and message passing?

c.x: Shared memory is managed by the OS and suits distributed environments; message passing needs a shared region
Both need a shared region, but only message passing uses a message queue in the kernel
Shared memory uses a region the processes read and write; message passing needs no shared memory and is managed by the OS
Message passing uses a region the processes read and write; shared memory uses send and receive operations

qs.e: In shared memory the processes read and write data in a common region. Message passing allows processes to communicate without sharing memory, is managed by the OS, and is useful in a distributed environment. Shared region vs OS-managed messages

qs.q: Which option correctly describes the trade-off between fixed-sized and variable-sized messages?

c.x: Fixed-sized: complex to implement but flexible for programmers; variable-sized: easy to implement but restrictive
Fixed-sized: easy to implement but restricts programmers; variable-sized: complex to implement but more flexible
Both are easy to implement, but only variable-sized messages restrict programmers
Both are complex to implement, but only fixed-sized messages are flexible for programmers

qs.e: Fixed-sized messages are easier to implement at the system level but restrict the application programmer. Variable-sized messages are more complex at the system level but make application programming easier and more flexible. <mark>System-level simplicity vs programmer flexibility</mark>

qs.q: Which of the following is <u>not</u> one of the logical implementation choices for a communication link?

c.x: Direct or indirect communication
Synchronous or asynchronous communication
Automatic or explicit buffering
Hardware bus or network connection

qs.e: A hardware bus or a network is a form of the physical implementation of a link. The logical choices are direct or indirect communication, synchronous or asynchronous communication, and automatic or explicit buffering. Bus and network are physical, not logical

qs.q: Process $P$ calls `send(Q, message)` and process $Q$ calls `receive(P, message)`. Which kind of communication is this?

c.x: Direct communication with symmetric addressing
Direct communication with asymmetric addressing
Indirect communication using a mailbox
Indirect communication using a port

qs.e: Both the sender and the receiver name each other, which is symmetric addressing in direct communication. In asymmetric addressing only the sender names the receiver, and the receiver accepts a message from any process. Direct, symmetric addressing

qs.q: Which of the following is <u>not</u> a property of a direct communication link?

c.x: A link is established automatically
A link is associated with exactly two processes
A link may be associated with more than two processes
Between each pair of processes there exists exactly one link

qs.e: A direct link is established automatically, is associated with exactly two processes, and there is exactly one link between each pair. A link that can involve more than two processes is an indirect (mailbox) link. More than two processes = indirect link

qs.q: Several processes communicate through a named object $A$ using `send(A, message)` and `receive(A, message)`. Which kind of communication is this, and what is $A$?

c.x: Direct communication, and A is a process
Indirect communication, and A is a mailbox (or port)
Direct communication, and A is a socket
Indirect communication, and A is a stub

qs.e: In indirect communication messages are sent to and received from mailboxes (or ports), and the link is established by creating and sharing a mailbox. Indirect communication through a mailbox

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares direct and indirect communication links?

c.x: A direct link joins exactly two processes; an indirect link may join more than two
A direct link may join more than two processes; an indirect link joins exactly two
A pair may have several direct links; an indirect link is created automatically
A direct link needs a mailbox; an indirect link is established automatically

qs.e: A direct link is established automatically between exactly two processes, with exactly one link per pair. An indirect link is created by sharing a mailbox, may involve more than two processes, and a pair may have several mailboxes. <mark>Direct: exactly two processes; indirect: possibly more</mark>

qs.q: A sending process hands over its message and resumes execution immediately, without waiting for the receiver. Which operation is this?

c.x: Blocking (synchronous) send
Blocking (synchronous) receive
Non-blocking (asynchronous) receive
Non-blocking (asynchronous) send

qs.e: A non-blocking (asynchronous) send sends the message and resumes operation immediately. A blocking send waits until the message is received by the receiver or by the mailbox. Non-blocking send

qs.q: Which option correctly describes when the sender blocks for each buffering capacity?

c.x: Zero: never blocks; bounded: blocks until the recipient receives; unbounded: blocks only when the queue is full
Zero: blocks only when the queue is full; bounded: never blocks; unbounded: blocks until the recipient receives
Zero: blocks until the recipient receives; bounded: blocks only when the queue is full; unbounded: never blocks
Zero: blocks until the recipient receives; bounded: never blocks; unbounded: blocks only when the queue is full

e: Zero capacity: the link cannot hold any waiting message, so the sender must block until the recipient receives it.
Bounded capacity: the queue holds at most $n$ messages, so the sender blocks only if the queue is full, until space is available.
Unbounded capacity: the queue length is infinite, so the sender never blocks.
<mark>Zero: blocks until received; bounded: blocks when full; unbounded: never blocks</mark>

qs.q: How is a socket identified?

c.x: By a process number concatenated with a mailbox name
By an IP address concatenated with a port number
By a stub identifier concatenated with a function identifier
By a host name concatenated with a PCB number

qs.e: A socket is an endpoint for communication, identified by an IP address concatenated with a port number. A pair of communicating processes employs a pair of sockets. IP address + port number

qs.q: In the lecture's sockets example, host $X$ (146.86.5.20) communicates with a web server (161.25.19.8). Which pair of sockets identifies this connection?
qs.e: Each socket is an IP address concatenated with a port number. Host $X$ uses the socket `146.86.5.20:1625`, and the web server uses the socket `161.25.19.8:80`, so the connection is identified by this pair. <mark>146.86.5.20:1625 ↔ 161.25.19.8:80</mark>

qs.q: How does a server handle client requests when it uses sockets?

c.x: It repeatedly connects to each client address to check whether a request is pending
It creates a mailbox for every client and waits for the clients to receive from it
It calls a remote procedure on the client through a stub on the client side
It listens to a specified port and accepts a connection when a request is received

qs.e: The server waits for client requests by listening to a specified port; when a request is received, it accepts a connection from the client socket. Listen on a port, then accept the connection

qs.q: What is the role of the stub on the client side of a remote procedure call (RPC)?

c.x: It listens to a port on the remote system and waits for incoming calls
It executes the remote function and returns the output to the client
It hides the communication details so the remote procedure is called like a local one
It guarantees that the remote procedure executes exactly once

qs.e: The client-side stub hides the communication details and allows the remote procedure to be called like a local one. Listening to a port is the job of the RPC daemon on the remote system. The stub hides the communication details

qs.q: Which of the following statements about RPC is <u>not</u> true?

c.x: An RPC daemon listens to a port on the remote system
An RPC is guaranteed to run exactly once despite network errors
The messages are well structured and carry the function identifier and parameters
The output of the executed function is returned to the client as a message

qs.e: RPCs may <u>fail</u> or execute multiple times because of network errors, so exactly-once execution is not guaranteed. The other statements match the lecture: a daemon listens on a port, messages contain the function identifier and parameters, and the output is returned as a message. <mark>RPCs may fail or run multiple times</mark>
